---
title: "Notes on performance metric and feature penalisation"
author: "J. Heffaran"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output: html_document

We proposed a penalisation to the performance metric of the following form: $$\text{penalisation term} = e^{-\lambda k_j}.$$

Thus the score for model j becomes:

$$\text{Score}(M_j) = \text{Pm}(M_j)e^{-\lambda k_j}.$$
This way of scoring our models is backed by at least some theory, if not somewhat losely.

First, what are we hoping to achieve with our score function? We want to select the best model out of our group. Our idea of the best model is one which predicts the rankings of teams accurately, espescially within the head and tail of the league table. This is captured by our Pm function. Further, we want a penalisation for the number of features a model uses for it's predictions. That is, if a complex model and a simple mode achieve similar predictive success, then we would want to choose the simpler model.

To achieve a balance between these objectives, we produced the above score function. It is a relativley natural function, where the lambda term has a somewhat nice interpretation when viewed through the lense of the bayesian model selection framework, which we will explore later. We choose our lambda value to have a meaningful penalisation over our proposed models.
That is $$P(M_j|D) \propto P(D|M_j)P(M_j).$$

Our scoring system is also somewhat similar to AIC. Note that if we take the log of our score, we get:

$$\ln(\text{Pm}(M_j)) - 0.02 k_j,$$
wheras AIC is given by:

$$\text{AIC} = 2k - 2\ln(\hat{\mathcal{L}})$$.

Note however, that rather than the likelihood function, our score measures model fit with our custom metric, and we also penalise the model complexity in a way more in keeping with our evaluation constraints.

Thus, although somewhat ad-hoc, our model selection score is similar in approach to that of AIC, and also has a somewhat nice intuition under the Bayesian framework.

We choose lambda = 0.02 so that the models which are more complex are penalised to some extent, but not so much so that we artifically force models to be overly simple. We expect this should strike a balance between over fitting and under fitting our models


Suppose we set our prior belief of model $M_j = e^{-\lambda k_j}$. We can then look to choose $\lambda$ with respect to our prior belief about the probability of the model $M_j$. That is, suppose for each feature which we could have chosen to include in our model, we have a uniform prior belief as to if we will include it $\mathbb{P}($include feature $l$ in mode$) = q_l$. Then we can also have $P(M_j) = e^{-\lambda k_j}\propto (\frac{q}{1-q})^{k_j}$. Thus we can rearange to find lambda in terms of our prior beliefs about any feature being included in our model. We have: $$\lambda = \ln(\frac{1-q}{q}).$$

Thus, if for each feature, we have the prior belief that it is to be included in our model just below half the time, ie $q = 0.495$, then we get $\lambda \approx 0.02$. This is a relativley mild penalisation but it is pretty apt for our case since we want to bound our model scores to $[0,1]$.

Note that in the context of the general bayesian framework, we now have $$P(M_j|D) \propto \text{Pm}(M_j)e^{-\lambda k_j}$$, which gives us our scoring system.

This gives us the adjusted pm:


```{r}
pm <- function(predicted, actual) {
  
  n <- length(actual)
  # Identify the top five teams
  P5 <- which(predicted <= 5)
  A5 <- which(actual <= 5)

  # Calculate overlap between predicted and actual top five
  overlap <- length(intersect(P5, A5)) / 5

  # Identify bottom three positions
  bottom3 <- (n - 2):n

  wt <- numeric(n)

  for (i in 1:n) {

    p <- predicted[i]
    a <- actual[i]

    d <- abs(p - a)

    if (a <= 5) { # Actual position is in the top five
      
      if (p == a) {
        w <- 1

      } else if (p <= 5) {
        w <- overlap

      } else {
        w <- -(1 - exp(-d))
      }

    } else {# Actual position is outside the top five

      if (a %in% bottom3) {# Actual team is in the bottom three

        if (p %in% bottom3) {
          w <- 1

        } else {
          w <- -(1 - exp(-d))
        }

      } else if (p <= 5) {# Incorrectly predicted in the top five
        
        w <- -(1 - exp(-d))

      } else if (p == a) {# Correctly predicted outside the top five

        w <- 0.5

      } else {# Incorrectly predicted outside the top five
        k <- 0.1
        w <- -(1 - exp(-k * d))
      }
    }

    wt[i] <- w
  }

  return(sum(wt))
}

```

We then feed this into our adjusted function to give our final score:

```{r}
pm_adjusted <- function(predicted, actual, number_features, lambda=0.01) {
  
  upper <- pm(predicted = epl_prediction$Actual_Rank, actual= epl_prediction$Actual_Rank)

lower <- pm(predicted = 21- epl_prediction$Actual_Rank,  actual= epl_prediction$Actual_Rank)

  prediction_score <- (pm(predicted, actual) -lower)/ (upper - lower)
  
  feature_penalisation <- exp(-lambda * number_features)
  
  model_score <- prediction_score * feature_penalisation
  
  return(model_score)
}

```
